summary: For ages 5-6 (UK Y1), learners add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers within 20, including the +0/−0 case, using known number bonds and making-ten rather than counting all. Core aims: fluent within-20 calculation, correct bridging across ten (e.g. 8+7), and understanding that adding or subtracting zero leaves a quantity unchanged. Activities centre on acting out calculations with ten-frames and number lines, with a concrete treatment of the zero case to dispel the belief that every operation must change the number.
misconceptions: Assuming +0 or −0 must change the number (giving 5+0=6 or 5−0=4).
Counting all/counting on in ones across the ten boundary instead of making ten.
Errors at the teen boundary (miscounting when crossing 10).
Ignoring the operation and just combining the two numbers seen.
Reversing subtraction to keep the larger number first without noticing the meaning changes.

activities.title: Drive a ten-frame and number-line calculator
steps: Build the first number on a double ten-frame (two ten-frames, since one frame holds only 10) (e.g. place eight counters on the first frame for 8+7).

Add or subtract the second number by moving counters, and for bridging cases split the second number to fill the frame to ten first (slide two counters over to complete ten, leaving five, to reach 15).
Show the same calculation as a jump on a 0-20 number line.
Write the matching number sentence alongside the action (e.g. 8 + 7 = 15).
Repeat with a non-bridging case (14 + 5) and a take-away (17 − 3).
activities.insight: Within-20 sums and differences can be found by using bonds and making ten, not by counting all in ones; bridging reorganises the quantity around ten.

activities.title: Add nothing, take nothing: the zero case
steps: Build a number on a double ten-frame (e.g. 12: one full frame and 2 on the second frame).
Choose 'add 0' and watch that no counters move and the number stays 12.
Choose 'subtract 0' from another number (e.g. 16) and confirm it stays 16.
Show the same on the number line as a jump of length zero that stays on the spot.
Say or write why the number did not change: adding or taking nothing leaves the quantity exactly as it was.
Contrast with a nearby case that does change (17 − 3 vs 17 − 0).
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting 0 leaves a number unchanged (n + 0 = n, n − 0 = n); not every operation changes the quantity.

activities.title: Spoken probe: what happens if we add zero?
steps: Discuss: 'What happens to 12 when you add nothing to it?'
Explain in your own words how 17 − 3 is different from 17 − 0.
Predict and justify the answer to a new zero case before checking it with objects.
activities.insight: Being able to state why adding or subtracting zero leaves a number unchanged shows understanding beyond getting the answer.

activities.title: Mixed within-20 practice set
steps: Work a varied set spanning non-bridging sums (14 + 5), bridging sums (8 + 7), take-aways (17 − 3, 15 − 7), and several +0/−0 items (12 + 0, 16 − 0).
Occasionally solve a missing-number item (e.g. 14 + ? = 19) to vary which quantity is unknown.
Jot a number line or ten-frame when helpful.

For non-bridging items, say which digit changed and which stayed the same (14 + 5 → the ones change, 4 + 5 = 9 → 19); notice that in bridging items like 8 + 7 the tens change too, and in ±0 items no digit changes.
activities.insight: Fluency comes from applying bonds and making-ten across the full 0-20 range, including the zero cases and the teen boundary.

checkQuestion: Work these out (you can jot or use a number line): 14 + 5? … 17 − 3? … 12 + 0? … 16 − 0?
checkAnswer: 19, 14, 12, 16 — the first two stay within the decade (add/subtract to the ones), and adding or subtracting 0 leaves the number unchanged.
